newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Videos force Brazil to confront police brutality.
newsitem.headline: Videos force Brazil to confront police brutality.

text.p: A report on brutality published on Tuesday brought fresh criticism against Brazilian police and added to public outrage over two videotapes showing police beating, kicking and shooting at civilians.

James Cavallaro, author of a 120-page report "Police Brutality in Urban Brazil" published by U.S.-based Human Rights Watch/Americas, said the tapes made people realise police violence could affect anyone anytime.
"The victims (in the videos) are 'good people,'" he said. "This fact has caused Brazilians to realise that we are all at risk of being the next victim."
He said many similar cases of abuses by the police had not provoked public outrage in the past because they involved criminals or individuals considered to be social outcasts.

Globo television aired one video showing military police in Sao Paulo beating drivers at a roadblock and firing at a car and another showing military police in Rio de Janeiro punching and kicking a group of men lined up against a wall. One of the car passengers later died.

The outcry caused by the videos prompted President Fernando Henrique Cardoso to sign a decree on Monday establishing a human rights watchdog and to sanction a bill making torture a crime for the first time.

The new Human Rights Secretariat will oversee the implementation of a landmark National Plan for Human Rights, and the new law punishes torture with jail sentences of two to eight years, rising to 16 years in fatal cases. Until now police and military officers accused of mistreating civilians and prisoners were punishable for the lesser crime of battery.

But Cardoso said he did not believe changing the law was enough to counteract police brutality because it was a cultural problem. "We are in a country which has always tended to accept police violence," he told the weekly Veja magazine. "There is no law that can change this overnight."
Cavallaro agreed that cultural attitudes in Brazil encouraged acts of police brutality but he insisted that new legislation could help curb police violence.

"We have been pleased with the steps taken by the executive branch of government but they haven't been matched by Congress," Cavallaro said. "We hope Congress will now be more willing to take steps to end police violence."
The Human Rights Watch/Americas report calls for Congress to approve the more than 200 measures that constitute the National Plan for Human Rights released by Cardoso last May.

Since then the government has had trouble getting Congress to approve implementing legislation including bills allowing for military police to be tried in the ordinary courts in cases of abuses against civilians and federal jurisdiction to apply in cases involving serious human rights violations.
The impunity most acts of police brutality enjoy is the single most important factor driving such abuse and is largely the result of an inadequate justice system, Cavallaro said.
